content: Cardiotocography (CTG) is a method used to continuously monitor the fetal heart rate by placing an ultrasound transducer on the mother’s abdomen. It is commonly employed during pregnancy to assess fetal well-being, particularly in cases where there is an increased risk of complications. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of antenatal CTG, including both traditional and computerised methods, in improving outcomes for mothers and their babies during and after pregnancy. The researchers conducted a systematic search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of June 26, 2015) and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. They included randomised and quasi-randomised trials that compared traditional CTG with no CTG or concealed CTG results, computerised CTG with no CTG or concealed CTG results, and computerised CTG with traditional CTG. Six studies involving a total of 2,105 women were included in the analysis. However, the overall quality of the studies was low, with only two studies demonstrating adequate randomisation sequence generation and allocation concealment. All included studies focused on women at increased risk of complications. When comparing traditional CTG with no CTG, there was no significant difference in perinatal mortality (risk ratio [RR] 2.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.95 to 4.42; 2.3% versus 1.1%; four studies, 1,627 women; low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in potentially preventable deaths (RR 2.46, 95% CI 0.96 to 6.30; four studies, 1,627 women). However, the meta-analysis was underpowered to reliably assess these outcomes. There was also no significant difference in the rate of caesarean sections (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.28; 19.7% versus 18.5%; three trials, 1,279 women; low-quality evidence). Secondary outcomes, such as Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.88; one trial, 396 women; very low-quality evidence) and admission to neonatal special care or intensive care units (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.39; two trials, 883 women; low-quality evidence), also showed no significant differences. Other secondary outcomes were similarly unaffected. No eligible studies were identified that compared computerised CTG with no CTG. When comparing computerised CTG with traditional CTG, there was a significant reduction in perinatal mortality with computerised CTG (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.88; 0.9% versus 4.2%; two studies, 469 women; moderate-quality evidence). However, there was no significant difference in potentially preventable deaths (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.04 to 1.29; two studies, 469 women), although the meta-analysis was underpowered to assess this outcome. There was no significant difference in the rate of caesarean sections (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.24; 63% versus 72%; one study, 59 women; low-quality evidence) or in Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.30 to 5.74; two studies, 469 women; very low-quality evidence). Secondary outcomes also showed no significant differences. In conclusion, there is no clear evidence that antenatal CTG improves perinatal outcomes. However, further research is needed, particularly focusing on the use of computerised CTG in specific populations of women at increased risk of complications.
